$comment: Conformance corpus of the scene event contract (docs/events-contract.json, prose in docs/events.md). Add a case here first; a runner that disagrees is the bug. Runners: frameos/src/frameos/tests/test_event_fixtures.nim (the Nim runtime every host compiles: allow-list, log policy, and what the interpreter does with a delivered event), embedded/esp32/main/tests/test_fos_events.c through backend/app/tasks/tests/test_esp32_events_contract.py (the firmware's C tables), backend/app/utils/tests/test_events_contract.py (the backend), cloud/apps/auth-web/src/test/events-contract.test.ts (the cloud's event route and schedule validator) and cloud/apps/auth-web/src/test/shared-spa/events-contract.test.ts (the shared SPA and the frameos-wasm package). `dispatcher`: frameos/src/frameos/tests/test_event_loop.nim — queueing, origins, the command/event split and the render rule, which every host gets from the one dispatcher. `inputState`: frameos/src/frameos/tests/test_input_state.nim — what the input state makes of button edges and time (frameos/src/frameos/input_state.nim), the same on every host.

origins.$comment: May `origin` emit `event`? Every origin is asked: the dispatcher stamps and checks each envelope. `allowed` is what an edge that cannot see the scene answers — the scheduler, a hub verb, the firmware's C table, a control plane's validator: for a custom event from an origin a scene can opt into (`customEvents.declarableOrigins`) that is true, and the dispatcher then asks the scene showing (see `dispatcher`).

cases.why: Same, for a reload of every scene.
The frame access key must not be able to reboot-loop the device.
A scene that restarts the runtime on every render is a boot loop anyone can publish.
The frame access key must not be able to reboot-loop the device.
Same, for the whole device.
The frame access key must not be able to reboot-loop the device.
Scene code is untrusted: it must not replace the installed scenes past the guards of the push path.
A schedule entry carries no origin stamp, so it would smuggle scenes past the guards of the push path.
The frame access key is printed on the frame's QR code; it picks scenes, it does not replace them.
The browser preview forwards the keyboard and the wheel of the focused canvas, as a frame's driver would.

cloudEventRoute.$comment: POST /api/frames/<id>/event/<event> on the cloud: the hub verb the event becomes, on which device profiles, for a frame reporting `frameosVersion` (absent = none reported, which counts as older than every `since`). `customEvents` is what the scene the frame is showing declares. Where there is no verb (verb null, or a profile not listed) the route answers `error`: 404 unsupported_event unless the case names another. `sceneEventCases`: what may ride `scene_event {name, payload?}` at all — `error` null = accepted, otherwise the token the cloud (and the device) answers.

sceneEventCases.name: nextPage
sceneEventCases.why: A custom name may ride the verb; whether the scene showing declares it is asked separately, and again by the device.

sceneEventCases.name: reboot
sceneEventCases.why: A device command has a verb and an audit line of its own; scene_event is not a second door to it.

sceneEventCases.why: Not an event the cloud origin may emit.

log.$comment: What the frame log says when a host drains `event` with `payload`: null = no line at all; without `payload` = the name only.

cases.why: A key is logged by name only: the log is stored by the control plane and may be sent to the cloud.
One per motion report: not logged at all.

sequences.$comment: A scene, then events delivered to it one by one. Per step: `listenersRun` = how many event nodes ran; `state` = a subset of the scene's state afterwards (null = not set); `queued` = what the scene dispatched, in order — exact, so [] means nothing; `logged` = log lines that must appear (subset match); `notLogged` = strings that must not appear in any log line of the step.

cases.name: a listener runs for its event and no other
cases.why: Delivery is by name: every event node whose keyword matches runs, nothing else does.

cases.name: every matching listener runs
cases.why: There is no `handled`: two listeners for one event both run (routing is docs/event-system-analysis.md §4.6).

cases.name: a filter is string equality on top-level payload keys
cases.why: An integer payload value matches its decimal spelling; a filtered-out event runs nothing and is reported once.

cases.name: the legacy button label filter still matches
cases.why: Scenes from before `data.config` keep their `data.label` filter on a button listener: aliases are forever.

cases.name: setSceneState applies public state and asks for a render only when told to
cases.why: `state` lands on the scene's state; `render` in the payload queues one render event.

cases.name: a custom event reaches its listener, from a dispatch node too
cases.why: A name that is not in the contract is a custom scene event: delivered by name, and a scene may dispatch it.

cases.name: a dispatch is queued, never run inside the handler
cases.why: What a handler dispatches is delivered after the run that dispatched it. At this level every host agrees; how each host drains the queue is where they differ today (docs/events.md, "Known host differences").

cases.name: a scene may not dispatch a device command
cases.why: The `scene` origin is on no device command but `metrics`: the dispatch is dropped and says so.

cases.name: render dispatched while rendering is ignored
cases.why: A render that asks for a render is a loop; every host drops it.

dispatcher.$comment: The shared dispatcher (frameos/src/frameos/event_loop.nim) with a recording host around the real interpreter. Per step: `send` = envelopes enqueued together (origin, event, payload), then ONE drain; or `renderPass` = the host renders the current scene and drains. `trace` = exactly what happened, in order: `run <scene> <event>` (add the payload as compact JSON to pin it), `refused <event> <origin> <reason>`, `command <name>`, `select <sceneId>` (` failed` when there is no such scene), `power on|off`, `pass <scene>` (a render pass) and `render` (the host was asked to render, once, after the drain). `state` = subset of the current scene's state (null = not set); `current` = the current scene id; `budget` / `handled` / `pending` = a drain with that budget delivered that many and left that many queued. The test frame is 4x3.

cases.name: a device command goes to the host and never to a scene
cases.why: `reload` is a RuntimeCommand: the host is asked, and an event node that listens for the name does not run.

cases.name: an origin that is not on the list is refused, whoever it is
cases.why: The allow-list is asked of every envelope in one place. The access key may not reboot, a driver may not switch scenes, nobody but the host says `open`.

cases.name: what a handler dispatches runs after it, and the state it changes is drawn
cases.why: Queued delivery on every host: `button` runs to its end, then the `nextPage` it dispatched. The render rule sees the state change and asks for one render — a button press is somebody else talking to the scene.

steps.why: The same press again changes nothing, so nothing is drawn.

cases.name: renderAfter is the contract's
cases.why: `never` for pointer events even when a handler changes state (a scene that wants a picture dispatches render); `always` for render; `if-state-changed` for the rest. Input reaches a scene only under the names it listens for (`keyUp` has a listener with nothing behind it; the `pointerDown` the `mouseDown` alias stands for has none, and is not run).

cases.name: a render that changes its own state does not cause the next render
cases.why: A slideshow's render dispatches setSceneState to turn its page. That is the scene talking to itself: were it to count as a state change, every render would cause another, forever, on an e-paper panel. It renders again only by dispatching `render`.

steps.why: The same dispatch from a button handler is a person's doing, and is drawn.

cases.name: a schedule or the cloud fires a custom event only at a scene that declares it
cases.why: Decision 5: `origins` on the custom event's declaration. The scene, the frame's own API and its drivers can always send it.

cases.name: a scene's own setCurrentScene switches scenes, on every host
cases.why: The host is asked to select; the scene left hears `close`, the one shown `open`. An unknown scene changes nothing.

cases.name: pointer moves coalesce, and input waits behind everything else
cases.why: `coalesce: latest` at enqueue: a move replaces the move it would queue behind. Two lanes: what a person did waits behind commands and scene traffic, in order within its lane. The scene listens for `mouseMove`, the old name of `pointerMove`: it hears the alias with the alias's payload — the position in scene pixels — and not the new name, which nothing listens for.

cases.name: turnOn and turnOff drive the display, then the scene hears them
cases.why: A scene command: the host acts, and a listener still runs.

cases.name: toggleScreen flips the display, and a touch on a dark screen only wakes it
cases.why: The dispatcher keeps whether the screen is on: a toggle turns it off when it is on and on when it is off, and the scene hears the turnOff or turnOn it became. A press on a dark screen turns it on and is nobody else's: its down, its up and whatever gesture it makes never reach the scene (nobody could see what they were pressing). The next press is the scene's again.

cases.name: a scene that re-dispatches its own event is handed back after a burst
cases.why: One drain delivers at most its budget and leaves the rest queued, so the host's render loop (or its one task) gets a turn. Nothing is dropped.

cases.name: an installed scene's event map rewrites what a button says before the scene hears it
cases.why: The map is the installed copy's (`eventMap` beside `nodes`, written by the control plane, kept across scene updates), applied by the dispatcher on every host before the scene is asked. A frame with a REFRESH key and a scene written for A and B: a press of REFRESH is the scene's A, a long press its B `press` (the rule writes `as` over the payload, action included), and the scene's own REFRESH listener never hears a mapped press. What no rule matches is delivered as it came, and a mapped `button` is logged as `event:mapped` with the rule's `as`, never the payload. Every rewrite is one `event:mapped` line (`scope: scene`).

cases.name: the frame's event map binds a press to the frame, whatever scene is showing
cases.why: frame.json `eventMap` is the control plane's "Button actions" (a reTerminal's LEFT and RIGHT held are the previous and the next scene, on every preset). The dispatcher applies it first, scene or no scene: a matching rule with `emit` replaces the press with the event it names (origin `eventMap`, `as` its payload) and the scene never hears the press — not even a listener with no filter; a rule without `emit` rewrites the payload for every scene. `setCurrentScene {direction}` walks the host's scene order (the control plane's list) and wraps; a direction that is not `next` or `prev` is refused. An installed scene's own rule may emit too (a double press of REFRESH is this scene's page 2). What the map emits is never mapped again.

cases.name: a long press bound to voiceChat is the host's device command, not the scene's press
cases.why: `voiceChat` (docs/voice-chat.md) is a device command only the frame's event map may emit, and only a key's long press makes sense of it. On the frame the firmware reads the binding off the map and opens the microphone while the key is held, claiming the press, so the rule never fires there; a long press the firmware did not take (a `button` said over HTTP, the preview, a Pi) runs through the dispatcher like any mapped press: replaced by `voiceChat` from origin `eventMap`, handed to the host as a device command, never to the scene, with no render. A short press of the same key is still the scene's. Said outright (`POST /event/voiceChat`), it is refused: the map is its only origin.

cases.name: a frame with one scene has no next scene
cases.why: `setCurrentScene {direction}` on a list of one resolves to the scene showing, and a switch to the scene showing without `state` changes nothing: no close, no open, no render. The preview is such a frame.

cases.name: the scene switcher opens from the scene showing, and the same again goes back
cases.why: `sceneSwitcher` is the dispatcher's to resolve, on every host: it selects the built-in scene `scenes.switcher` with `state.from`, the scene showing, and while the switcher shows it selects that scene again. A touch screen's event map binds it to a swipe in from the bottom edge. While the switcher shows, `setCurrentScene {direction}` walks the list from the scene it was opened from, and a `setCurrentScene` to the switcher by name carries `state.from` too. In the switcher a key with the role `next` moves the highlight one scene on, and one with the role `refresh` (or `primary`) shows the highlighted scene: the switcher dispatches `setCurrentScene` for it. The switcher is in no scene list.

inputState.$comment: The input state's button half (frameos/src/frameos/input_state.nim), alone, on one pin (GPIO 6, label B, role next by label) unless a case says otherwise. Per step: `at` = the runner's clock in ms when the step happens; `send` = one `gpio` (an edge) or `button` payload applied at that time, or `tick` = time passing. `atMs` values in payloads are on the same clock as `at` (the runner shifts both onto its monotonic clock). `delivered` = exactly what came out, in order: event name, and a subset of the payload.

cases.name: a tap is down and up at once, and a press when its window closes
cases.why: The hardware layer is immediate. The button layer waits doublePressMs (350) after the up for a second down; none came, so the tap is a press, carrying its down's atMs and how long it was.

cases.name: a fast double tap is one doublePress and no press
cases.why: Two 40 ms taps 100 ms apart, as a thumb does them. The second down is the doublePress; the pair is that and nothing more.

cases.name: the down that closes the window is the double press, the one after it starts over
cases.why: A second down exactly doublePressMs after the up still pairs. A third down right after a double press is a new first tap.

cases.name: a slow second tap is two presses
cases.why: The window closed between the taps: the first is a press on the tick, the second its own.

cases.name: a tap made during a render is a tap
cases.why: The ESP32 drains its button queue between render passes. Both edges arrive 30 s late; the hold is the 200 ms between their stamps, and the next tick makes it a press, not a long press.

cases.name: a double tap during a render is a doublePress
cases.why: The four edges arrive together after the refresh; their stamps say the second down came 100 ms after the first up.

cases.name: two slow taps during a render are two presses, in order
cases.why: The first tap's window closed before the second down: it is delivered as a press before that down, then the second becomes one on the tick.

cases.name: a hold is one longPress, on its up
cases.why: Nothing is delivered while the key is down, however long. The up decides: held at least longPressMs (1000), it is a longPress, after the up, with the same duration and the down's atMs. A long press is not also a press.

cases.name: a hold through a render is a longPress
cases.why: Both edges sat in the queue; their stamps say the key was down 2.5 s.

cases.name: a key still held when the render ends makes nothing until its up
cases.why: The down was queued at 1000 and drained at 30000 with the key still down: no tick makes anything of a hold; the up does.

cases.name: a hold just short of longPressMs is a press, and one exactly that long a longPress
cases.why: The line is longPressMs held: 999 ms is a short press (it waits for a second down, then is a press), 1000 ms a long one.

cases.name: the second down of a double press makes no longPress
cases.why: Each press is exactly one of press, doublePress or longPress: a double press held is still a double press, and its up makes nothing more.

cases.name: the tap that woke the device is a press like any other
cases.why: An ESP32 cannot see its keys while it boots (about a second). A wake key already up by then was a tap: the button task stamps its down and up when it first saw them (1180), and the scene's first pass, seconds later, gets down, up, and the press once the window is over, marked wake.

cases.name: a hold that woke the device is a longPress
cases.why: Still down when the button task first looks: the press began at the reset (atMs 0), so the hold counts from there, and its up makes the longPress the finger meant.

cases.name: a double press can start with the tap that woke the device
cases.why: The wake tap's up is stamped when the button task first saw it (1180); a second down within doublePressMs of that pairs with it.

cases.name: an edge with no stamp is timed when it arrives
cases.why: A driver or a preview that gives no atMs: the hold is the time between deliveries.

cases.name: two buttons with no pin are two keys
cases.why: The preview's buttons have no GPIO line, so every one is pin -1; a key is its pin and its label. A tap on A and then one on B inside A's window is two presses, each when its own window closes, not a doublePress of B.

cases.name: a stamp from the future is now
cases.why: A clock the dispatcher does not share (atMs ahead of its own): the edge is timed at delivery, and its atMs passed on as it came.

cases.name: someone else's press is delivered as said
cases.why: HTTP, the cloud, a schedule or a scene saying a button was pressed moved no line and has nothing to time: no action is a press, at once; a named action is that action.

cases.name: an older producer's button edges are gpio edges
cases.why: Producers until 2026.10.16 sent their edges as `button`, with a `level` (and before that named them press / release). The level decides: a `gpio` down and up, and the `button` press they add up to.

cases.name: a button with the action down or up is an edge too
cases.why: A `button` naming the action `down` or `up` and no level (a page or a script from before `gpio`) is the edge it names.

cases.name: a gpio that names no edge is dropped
cases.why: `gpio` is a line moving: without a `level` or the action `down` / `up` it says nothing happened, and nothing is delivered.

cases.name: a press the frame claimed makes no button
cases.why: A key whose long press the frame's event map binds to `voiceChat` (REFRESH on a reTerminal E1001/E1002) starts the voice chat at the hold, docs/voice-chat.md: the frame took the press, so its `up` edge says `claimed` and the button layer makes no `longPress` of a hold that was a sentence, nor a `press` of a short one. The edges themselves are delivered, as every edge is. (The case holds two keys at once, as the chord that came before the binding did; one claimed key is the same rule once.)

cases.name: a short claimed press makes no press either
cases.why: A claimed key that let go early still answers to the frame (the firmware claims a voice key from the hold's start, whatever the key then does): `claimed` on its `up` ends the key without a `press`, so the scene does not flip a page because the frame started listening.
